In Europe, pedestrian crossings are typically white; Switzerland is one of the few countries that uses bold yellow bars almost universally on urban streets. The right-hand traffic, European-style bollards, and general Central European architecture further support Switzerland over neighboring countries like France, Germany, or Italy. City level: Overhead dual catenary wires run above the carriageway, but there are no rail tracks in the asphalt—this indicates a trolleybus corridor rather than a tramway. Several Swiss cities operate trolleybuses (e.g., Zürich, Geneva, Lausanne, Bern, Winterthur). The combination of dense midrise buildings, clean streets, German-speaking urban design cues, and a wooded hill rising at the end of the street point toward Zürich, which frequently presents views toward the Uetliberg/forested ridges from inner neighborhoods. Geneva and Lausanne often show French-language signage and lakefront topography, while Bern’s old town has arcades and sandstone; those traits aren’t visible here. Street level: The scene shows a multi-lane arterial with repeated yellow crosswalk bars spanning a wide intersection, a solid yellow side line consistent with a bus-priority edge, standard Swiss grey bollards with red reflective caps on the sidewalk, and trolleybus wires aligned along the street center. These elements together suggest a Zürich inner-city arterial served by trolleybuses rather than a tram corridor, narrowing to streets in districts like Aussersihl or Wiedikon where such infrastructure is common. Exact street identification is uncertain without readable signage, but the combination of markings, wires, and backdrop hill is distinctive of Zürich’s inner districts.
